sbh3.1:2.2: The nine *cittasthiti* are named by nine distinct Sanskrit verbs sharing the root √sthā (to stand, to place), prefixed to mark stages: *sthāpayati* (places — initial binding), *saṁsthāpayati* (places continuously — refines the binding), *avasthāpayati* (places again — recovers after drift), *upasthāpayati* (places closely — secures after recovery), *damayati* (tames — checks the pull of distracting signs), *śamayati* (pacifies — checks the pull of distracting thoughts/defilements), *vyupaśamayati* (fully pacifies — refuses to tolerate occurrences when they slip through), *ekotī-karoti* (makes single-pointed — sustains uninterrupted flow with effort), *samādhatte* (concentrates — sustains the same flow effortlessly). The progression is *not* nine distinct meditation techniques but nine increasingly subtle stages of the *same* mind-binding operation. Adopted verbatim by Kamalaśīla's *Bhāvanākrama* and through it into the entire Tibetan *lam rim* literature; cited (with the same nine names) in Asaṅga's *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* XIV.
sbh3.1:3.2: *upanibadhnāti* literally means 'binds' or 'ties up' — the mind is tied to the object the way a rope is tied to a stake. More active than the English 'places'.
sbh3.1:4.2: The first stage's binding is described as *balam audārikam asaṁsthitam* — strong, gross, unsettled. Stage 2 refines that crude holding into something more subtle and gathered, on the same object.
sbh3.1:6.4: *ādīnava-saṁjñā* (perception of danger) is the operative tool, already cultivated previously. The practitioner doesn't suppress distractions through force; recognition of their danger does the work.
sbh3.1:6.5: *prasaraṁ na dadāti* — 'does not give them spreading-room.' The distractions still arise but are not allowed to expand.
sbh3.1:9.2: Three adjectives describe the flow at this stage: *niścchidra* (without gaps), *nirantara* (uninterrupted), and the flow is of *samādhi* itself. The qualifier *sābhisaṁskāraṁ* — 'with effort' — distinguishes stage 8 from stage 9.
sbh3.1:10.2: *anābhoga* and *anabhisaṁskāra* — 'without exertion' and 'without deliberate effort.' The decisive contrast with stage 8. There is no new technique at stage 9; just the natural maturing of what was practiced at stage 8.
sbh3.1:11.2: The original enumeration at 11.2 lists only four — 'hearing-and-thinking,' mindfulness, diligence, familiarity — but the body of the chapter (¶12) clearly distinguishes six: śruta-bala and cintā-bala (separately at 12.1–4 via the 'taking what he has heard *and* what he has reflected on'), smṛti-bala (12.5–6), samprajanya-bala (12.7–8), vīrya-bala (12.9–11), and paricaya-bala (12.12). Restored in brackets. The same six-fold list — with the same internal mapping — appears in Asaṅga's *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* XIV.13 and in Kamalaśīla's *Bhāvanākrama* III. Note the deliberate pairing: 1 power → 2 stages; 1 power → 2 stages; 1 power → 2 stages; 1 power → 2 stages; 1 power → 1 stage; 1 power → 1 stage — giving 6×(2,2,2,2,1,1) = 9.
sbh3.1:13.2: The four *manaskāra* — *bala-vāhana* (force-borne), *sacchidra-vāhana* (interrupted-borne), *niścchidra-vāhana* (uninterrupted-borne), *anābhoga-vāhana* (effortless-borne) — are mapped one-to-many onto the nine *cittasthiti* at 14.1–4: stages 1–2 are force-borne, stages 3–7 are interrupted-borne, stage 8 is uninterrupted-borne, stage 9 is effortless-borne. This mapping is the structural counterpart to [sbh2.0:59.119](sbh2.0.html#sbh2.0:59.119), where the same four *manaskāra* were introduced abstractly; here they are tied concretely to the nine stages. The same four reappear at the corresponding *vipaśyanā* stages at 15.2–3 — calm and insight share the same architecture of mental engagement.
sbh3.1:15.2: The hinge from śamatha to vipaśyanā is structural, not technical: the *same* four *manaskāra* are reused; the *same* nine-stage progression applies. What differs is the *object*. On the śamatha side, the object is a single chosen meditation-object held with one-pointedness; on the vipaśyanā side, the object is the four-fold support of wisdom (which the chapter does not unpack here — it is treated in [sbh3.2](sbh3.2.html)). The bridge is one of the chapter's most important architectural moves: it positions the nine-stage *cittasthiti* as not merely a śamatha-development scheme but as the *general* form of attention-stabilization, applicable equally to insight cultivation.
